Chapter 3: The Link Between Dismissal and Violence—How Culture Enables Harm
There’s a thread connecting all those moments when women are talked over, doubted, or ignored—a thread that, if you follow it, leads to something much darker.
See, the habit of brushing off women’s voices isn’t just about awkward conversations or feeling left out. It shapes lives, and it creates the kind of environment where real harm can take root—protected by disbelief and denial.
Think about how we usually talk about violence against women. When a story breaks—about an assault or someone going missing—how fast does the focus turn to what the victim did? What was she wearing? Why was she out so late? Did she know the person? The questions just pile up, don’t they? And each one quietly suggests that the responsibility is hers, not the perpetrator’s.
The message comes through loud and clear: women are somehow to blame for what happens to them, or at the very least, they can’t be trusted to tell the truth about their own lives.
This kind of thinking isn’t just in headlines or tabloid stories. It slips into police reports, courtrooms, and even the way we talk to each other every day. When a woman reports harassment or abuse, too often she’s met with disbelief—or just plain indifference. Authorities might downplay what happened, suggest she’s overreacting, or not even bother to investigate properly. Sometimes, the very process of seeking justice turns into a whole new trauma, forcing women to relive their pain in spaces that feel anything but safe.
The impact? It’s devastating. When women aren’t believed, those who hurt them feel untouchable. The message gets out: you can get away with it. And so, the cycle continues—silence and disbelief making it even easier for abuse to go on. This isn’t just about individual cases; it’s a systemic problem, showing us a culture that puts men’s perspectives first and cares more about protecting reputations than finding the truth.
Let me share a story that brings this home. Imagine a woman who’s endured years of abuse. She finally finds the courage to go to the police. She tells her story, only to be met with skepticism. The officers ask if she’s really sure, if maybe she’s exaggerating, or if she somehow provoked it. The investigation goes nowhere. In the end, she feels more alone than ever, and the person who hurt her faces no consequences—free to keep going as if nothing happened.
Sadly, this isn’t some rare event. All around the world, women face the same barriers when they try to get help. The numbers are staggering: most sexual assaults aren’t reported, and of those that are, few lead to convictions. There are a lot of reasons for this, but at the heart of it is a simple, painful truth: when women aren’t believed, justice just isn’t possible.
The connection between being dismissed and being hurt isn’t always obvious. It starts small—an interruption here, a doubt there—and then it grows. When women’s voices are constantly undervalued, it becomes all too easy to overlook their pain, to ignore their suffering, to let those who harm them off the hook. Disbelief isn’t just rude—it can be deadly.
But there are signs things are changing. More and more women are speaking out, sharing their stories, demanding to be heard. Movements are growing, powered by the courage to tell the truth and the refusal to be silenced. In these moments, telling your story isn’t just brave—it’s a form of resistance. And it shows us something really important: the very first step to ending violence is to truly listen—and to believe.
We’re not there yet. Old habits of dismissal and disbelief run deep, shaped by centuries of tradition and power. But with every story shared, every act of solidarity, the culture shifts just a little.
One day, the hope is that women won’t have to fight to be heard—and that justice won’t depend on whether someone else is willing to listen.
